headline: Connecticut RealPage rent-pricing case will continue after court ruling
dek: A federal antitrust lawsuit backed by Connecticut and other states survived RealPage's effort to have the case thrown out, keeping allegations about algorithmic rent setting in court.
body: Connecticut's antitrust case against RealPage will continue after a court rejected the company's attempt to have the rent-pricing lawsuit thrown out, Attorney General William Tong's office announced Tuesday. The ruling keeps alive a multistate challenge to software that prosecutors say helped landlords use nonpublic market information to coordinate apartment prices.

The [Connecticut Office of the Attorney General](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/court-sides-with-attorney-general-tong-in-realpage-case) said Connecticut, the U.S. Department of Justice and other states sued RealPage in 2024. The case alleges that RealPage sold revenue-management software to property managers, collected sensitive information about rents, discounts and available units, and used that information to recommend prices. State officials further allege that the system encouraged property managers to accept recommendations automatically, reducing the incentive to compete for renters.

Those are allegations, not findings that RealPage or the landlords violated the law. The ruling is a decision about whether the claims can proceed, not a final judgment on liability or a determination that any particular Connecticut tenant was overcharged. RealPage has not been found liable in the state announcement, and the public release did not identify the judge or provide a full copy of the order.

The litigation also includes six large landlord defendants named in a January 2025 amended complaint: Greystar Real Estate Partners, Blackstone's LivCor, Camden Property Trust, Cushman & Wakefield, Pinnacle Property Management Services and Willow Bridge Property Company. The attorney general's office said the coalition alleges those companies worked with RealPage and each other by sharing competitively sensitive information and using common pricing tools. A prior state announcement identified Greystar, Pinnacle and Willow Bridge as companies operating in Connecticut, giving the case a direct connection to renters in the state.

Two of those landlord matters have already taken a different path. Tong's office said Connecticut joined other attorneys general in settlements totaling $7 million with LivCor and $7 million with Greystar. Under those agreements, the companies agreed to stop using nonpublic data from other landlords to set rents. The settlements do not resolve the remaining case against RealPage or answer the broader question of how algorithmic pricing affects apartment markets.

The [Justice Department's case page](https://www.justice.gov/atr/case/us-and-plaintiff-states-v-realpage-inc) identifies the case as *U.S. and Plaintiff States v. RealPage, Inc.* and lists Connecticut among the state plaintiffs. Its docket materials include the 2024 complaint, an amended complaint and filings related to proposed judgments involving several landlord defendants. The federal record shows the case has generated separate resolutions and ongoing claims rather than one single proceeding with one outcome for every defendant.

The dispute matters in Connecticut because rent-setting decisions can affect the starting price, renewal price and discounts offered at multifamily properties, even when the software company and property owner are not household names to tenants. The state's case does not establish how much any Connecticut renter paid because of the alleged conduct, and the attorney general's announcement did not provide a statewide damages estimate. It does show what the state is seeking: an order preventing RealPage and participating property managers from sharing nonpublic information and working together to inflate rents.

Renters should not treat the Tuesday ruling as an immediate rent reduction or a payment announcement. A surviving lawsuit can move into further litigation, settlement discussions or trial, and the public sources reviewed for this report do not establish a final remedy or timeline. For now, Connecticut remains one of the states pursuing the case, while the next major developments will come through court filings, additional settlements or a final decision on the allegations.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut RealPage rent-pricing antitrust case continues
seoDescription: Connecticut's antitrust case against RealPage survived a motion to dismiss, keeping allegations about algorithmic rent pricing in court.
